source: (4) ectepicondylar groove on humerus present (like in Largocephalosaurus qianensis, absent in L. polycarpon)
evidence: This is part of the formal diagnosis based on specimen observation.

claim: Prosaurosphargis has an entepicondylar foramen in the humerus absent.
source: (5) entepicondylar foramen in humerus absent (as in Largocephalosaurus) (details of humerus morphology unknown in Sinosaurosphargis)
evidence: This is part of the formal diagnosis based on specimen observation.

claim: Prosaurosphargis has a radius short relative to humerus compared with other saurosphargids.
source: (6) radius short relative to humerus compared with other saurosphargids
evidence: This is part of the formal diagnosis based on specimen observation and comparison.

claim: Prosaurosphargis has a single distal tarsal (distal tarsal IV).
source: (7) presence of a single distal tarsal (distal tarsal IV) (different from Largocephalosaurus, which possesses two distal tarsals – III and IV) (number of tarsals unknown in Sinosaurosphargis)
evidence: This is part of the formal diagnosis based on specimen observation.

claim: Prosaurosphargis has anterior caudal ribs shorter than sacral ribs.
source: (8) anterior caudal ribs shorter than sacral ribs (anterior caudal ribs longer than sacral ribs in Largocephalosaurus, unknown in Sinosaurosphargis).
evidence: This is part of the formal diagnosis based on specimen observation.

claim: Based on humerus:total body length and femur:total body length ratios, the total length of HFUT YZSB-19-109 is estimated to have reached between 1468 mm to 1583 mm.
source: Based on the humerus:total body length and femur:total body length ratios of the type specimen of Largocephalosaurus qianensis (specimen IVPP V 15638, total body length = 2317 mm; Li et al., 2014), the only completely preserved saurosphargid specimen discovered to date, the total length of HFUT YZSB-19-109 is estimated to have reached between 1468 mm to 1583 mm, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with Largocephalosaurus qianensis.

claim: The transverse processes of cervical neural arches extend posterolaterally and are proportionally shorter than the transverse processes of the dorsal neural arches.
source: The transverse processes of the cervical neural arches extend posterolaterally and are proportionally shorter than the transverse processes of the dorsal neural arches.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claim: The dorsal centrum is mediolaterally constricted at its anteroposterior mid-length, resembling the dorsal centra of other saurosphargids.
source: It is mediolaterally constricted at its anteroposterior mid-length, resembling the dorsal centra of other saurosphargids (Huene, 1936; Li et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other saurosphargids.

claim: The maximum width of the transverse process is greater than the maximum width of the space between the transverse processes of adjacent neural arches.
source: The maximum width of the transverse process is greater than the maximum width of the space between the transverse processes of adjacent neural arches (Figure 3), a condition similar to that exhibited by Saurosphargis (Huene, 1936) and Sinosaurosphargis (Li et al., 2011), but different from Largocephalosaurus (Li et al., 2014) and Eusaurosphargis (Scheyer et al., 2017), in which the widths of the spaces between the dorsal transverse processes are approximately equal or greater than the widths of the transverse processes.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen (Figure 3) and comparison with other taxa.

claim: Articulated anterior and posterior dorsal neural arches preserved without their respective centra indicate a lack of fusion of the neurocentral suture.
source: Articulated anterior and posterior dorsal neural arches preserved without their respective centra indicate a lack of fusion of the neurocentral suture, a paedomorphic feature characteristic for Sauropterygia (Rieppel, 2000a) and also present in Saurosphargis (Huene, 1936) and Largocephalosaurus (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claim: Lack of fusion of the neurocentral suture is a paedomorphic feature characteristic for Sauropterygia.
source: Articulated anterior and posterior dorsal neural arches preserved without their respective centra indicate a lack of fusion of the neurocentral suture, a paedomorphic feature characteristic for Sauropterygia (Rieppel, 2000a) and also present in Saurosphargis (Huene, 1936) and Largocephalosaurus (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rieppel, 2000a.

claim: The caudal centra have concave lateral and ventral surfaces and are likely amphicoelus.
source: The sacral and caudal centra have concave lateral and ventral surfaces and are likely amphicoelus, as evidenced by the concave anterior articular surface of the second caudal centrum
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claim: A slightly rugose/striated dorsal surface is present in some of the anterior caudal neural spines, reminiscent of a similar surface present in the dorsal neural spines of Helveticosaurus, Augustasaurus, Nothosaurus, and Pomolispondylus.
source: A slightly rugose/striated dorsal surface, reminiscent of a similar surface present in the dorsal neural spines of Helveticosaurus (Rieppel, 1989a), Augustasaurus (Sander et al., 1997), Nothosaurus (Klein et al., 2022), and Pomolispondylus (Cheng et al., 2022), is preserved in some of the anterior caudal neural spines.
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claim: The anterior dorsal ribs have a single head and greatly expanded distal portions that abut against each other, forming a characteristic 'rib-basket'.
source: They have a single head and greatly expanded distal portions that abut against each other, forming a characteristic 'rib-basket' also present in other saurosphargids (Huene, 1936; Li et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014), but differ from the dorsal ribs of Eusaurosphargis, which are narrow and widely spaced (Scheyer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claim: The dorsal ribs do not bear a distinct uncinate process, being similar to Sinosaurosphargis but different from Largocephalosaurus, Saurosphargis, Eusaurosphargis and a possible isolated saurosphargid rib from the Late Triassic of Switzerland.
source: The dorsal ribs do not bear a distinct uncinate process, being similar in this respect to the dorsal ribs of Sinosaurosphargis (Li et al., 2011), but differ from the dorsal ribs of Largocephalosaurus, Saurosphargis, Eusaurosphargis and a possible isolated saurosphargid rib from the Late Triassic of Switzerland, all of which possess uncinate processes (Li et al., 2014; Scheyer et al., 2017; Scheyer et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claim: The anterior caudal ribs in HFUT YZSB-19-109 are shorter than the sacral ribs, in contrast to Largocephalosaurus.
source: The anterior caudal ribs in HFUT YZSB-19-109 are shorter than the sacral ribs, in contrast to Largocephalosaurus, in which the anterior caudal ribs are longer than the sacral ribs (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with Largocephalosaurus.

claim: Each gastral rib in HFUT YZSB-19-109 was composed of five elements – a median element, two lateral (first lateral) elements and two lateralmost (second lateral) elements.
source: Like in Eusaurosphargis, Placodus and eosauropterygians (Drevermann, 1933; Rieppel, 1989b; Nosotti and Rieppel, 2003; Shang et al., 2011), each gastral rib was composed of five elements – a median element, two lateral (first lateral) elements and two lateralmost (second lateral) elements.
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claim: The scapula of HFUT YZSB-19-109 closely resembles the scapula of Largocephalosaurus and Corosaurus in general shape and proportions.
source: In general shape and proportions, the scapula of HFUT YZSB-19-109 closely resembles the scapula of Largocephalosaurus (Cheng et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014) and Corosaurus (Storrs, 1991)
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claim: The coracoid of HFUT YZSB-19-109 closely resembles the coracoid of Largocephalosaurus.
source: The preserved parts of both coracoids indicate that it was a dorsoventrally flat, plate-like element, approximately sub-circular in outline, closely resembling the coracoid of Largocephalosaurs (Li et al., 2014; Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with Largocephalosaurus.

claim: The coracoid of HFUT YZSB-19-109 differs from the coracoids of Helveticosaurus, Eusaurosphargis, Atopodentatus, early diverging placodonts, Majiashanosaurus, a referred specimen of Hanosaurus, and Lariosaurus sanxiaensis.
source: The coracoid of HFUT YZSB-19-109 differs, however, from the coracoids of Helveticosaurus (Rieppel 1989), Eusaurosphargis, Atopodentatus, early diverging placodonts, Majiashanosaurus, a referred specimen of Hanosaurus, and Lariosaurus sanxiaensis, in which the coracoid is proximodistally more elongate and approximately sub-oval in outline (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claim: The humerus of HFUT YZSB-19-109 is posteriorly curved along its proximodistal axis, like the humerus of other saurosphargids, Placodus, Majiashanosaurus, Lariosaurus sanxiaensis, a referred specimen of Hanosaurus and numerous eosauropterygians.
source: The humerus is proximodistally elongate; it is also posteriorly curved along its proximodistal axis, like the humerus of other saurosphargids (Li et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2012), Placodus (Jiang et al., 2008), Majiashanosaurus (Jiang et al., 2014), Lariosaurus sanxiaensis (Li and Liu, 2020), a referred specimen of Hanosaurus (Wang et al., 2022) and numerous eosauropterygians (Rieppel, 1994).
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claim: The anterior margin of the humerus in HFUT YZSB-19-109 is not convex, but straight, making it more similar to the humeri of Placodus and Nothosaurus.
source: However, in contrast to Largocephalosaurus, the anterior margin of the humerus is not convex, but straight, making it more similar to the humeri of Placodus and Nothosaurus (Rieppel, 1994).
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claim: The radius/humerus proximodistal length ratio in HFUT YZSB-19-109 is ~0.55.
source: The radius/humerus proximodistal length ratio in HFUT YZSB-19-109 is ~0.55, in line with Eusaurosphargis (~0.51–0.57; Scheyer et al., 2017) and Placodus (~0.56; Jiang et al., 2008), but is significantly smaller than the ratio in Sinosaurosphargis (~0.66; Li et al., 2011), Largocephalosaurus polycarpon (~0.74; Cheng et al., 2012), L. qianensis (~0.67–0.72; Li et al., 2014), a referred specimen of Hanosaurus (~0.67; Wang et al., 2022), and Majiashanosaurus (~0.74; Jiang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on measurements of the specimen and comparison with other taxa.

claim: HFUT YZSB-19-109 had a proportionally shorter forearm compared with other saurosphargids and early eosauropterygians.
source: This indicates that HFUT YZSB-19-109 had a proportionally shorter forearm compared with other saurosphargids and early eosauropterygians.
evidence: This is inferred from the radius/humerus ratio comparison.

claim: The ilium of HFUT YZSB-19-109 is very similar to the ilia of Largocephalosaurus, Eusaurosphargis, Placodus, and Corosaurus.
source: The ilium of HFUT YZSB-19-109 is very similar to the ilia of Largocephalosaurus (Li et al., 2014), Eusaurosphargis (Nosotti and Rieppel, 2003), Placodus (Rieppel, 1995), and Corosaurus (Storrs, 1991), which all possess a well-developed, posteriorly projecting iliac blade.
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with other taxa.

claim: The pubis of HFUT YZSB-19-109 resembles the pubis of Largocephalosaurus in outline and proportions.
source: The pubis of HFUT YZSB-19-109 resembles the pubis of Largocephalosaurus (Li et al., 2014) in outline and proportions.
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison with Largocephalosaurus.

claim: The humerus/femur ratio in HFUT YZSB-19-109 is ~1.19.
source: The humerus/femur ratio in HFUT YZSB-19-109 is ~1.19, which is similar to the ratio in Largocephalosaurus (~1.20; Li et al., 2014), but is significantly greater than the ratio in Helveticosaurus (~1.11; Rieppel 1989), Placodus (~1.05; Jiang et al., 2008), and Eusaurosphargis (~0.89; Scheyer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on measurements of the specimen and comparison with other taxa.

claim: The phylogenetic analysis recovered 48 most parsimonious trees (MPTs) of 1008 steps each (CI = 0.272, RI = 0.620).
source: The phylogenetic analysis recovered 48 most parsimonious trees (MPTs) of 1008 steps each (CI = 0.272, RI = 0.620) (Figure 8).
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Prosaurosphargis was recovered as a member of Saurosphargidae, forming a polytomy with Sinosaurosphargis and Largocephalosaurus.
source: Prosaurosphargis was recovered as a member of Saurosphargidae, forming a polytomy with Sinosaurosphargis and Largocephalosaurus.
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Saurosphargidae is supported by three unambiguous synapomorphies: dorsal ribs transversely broadened and in antero-posterior contact with each other, forming closed 'rib-basket'; lateral gastralia expanded and flat; distal end of ulna distinctly expanded.
source: Saurosphargidae is supported by the following three unambiguous synapomorphies: dorsal ribs transversely broadened and in antero-posterior contact with each other, forming closed 'rib-basket' (char. 135.1); lateral gastralia expanded and flat (char. 141.1); distal end of ulna distinctly expanded (char. 167.1).
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Saurosphargidae was recovered within Sauropterygia, as the sister-group to the lineage leading to Eosauropterygia.
source: Saurosphargidae was recovered within Sauropterygia, as the sister-group to the lineage leading to Eosauropterygia.
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The saurosphargid-eosauropterygian clade is supported by six unambiguous synapomorphies.
source: The saurosphargid-eosauropterygian clade is supported by six unambiguous synapomorphies: frontal, butterfly-shaped with antero- and postero-lateral processes absent (ch. 29.0); long postorbital posterior process contacting squamosal (ch. 32.0); mandibular articulations displaced to a level distinctly behind occipital condyle (ch. 87.1); neural canal evenly proportioned (ch. 122.0); three sacral ribs (ch. 130.1); total number of carpal ossifications more than three (ch. 194.0).
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Pomolispondylus was recovered as the most basal member of the grade leading to Eosauropterygia.
source: Pomolispondylus, recently proposed as a sister-taxon of Saurosphargidae (Cheng et al., 2022), was recovered as the most basal member of the grade leading to Eosauropterygia
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The type and referred specimens of Hanosaurus were not unambiguously recovered in a monophyletic group.
source: The type (Rieppel, 1998a) and referred (Wang et al., 2022) specimens of Hanosaurus were not unambiguously recovered in a monophyletic group
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Corosaurus was recovered as the earliest-diverging member of Eosauropterygia.
source: Corosaurus was recovered as the earliest-diverging member of Eosauropterygia
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Wumengosaurus was recovered outside of the clade comprising pachypleurosaurs, nothosaurs and pistosaurs.
source: whereas Wumengosaurus was recovered outside of the clade comprising pachypleurosaurs, nothosaurs and pistosaurs.
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Atopodentatus was recovered as the sister-taxon of placodonts within Placodontiformes.
source: The herbivorous sauropterygian Atopodentatus was recovered as the sister-taxon of placodonts (represented in our dataset by Paraplacodus and Placodus) within Placodontiformes
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Placodontiformes is supported by four unambiguous synapomorphies: contact of the prefrontal and postfrontal excluding frontal from dorsal orbital margin; interpterygoid vacuity absent; splenial entering mandibular symphysis; and femur internal trochanter well developed.
source: supported by four unambiguous synapomorphies: contact of the prefrontal and postfrontal excluding frontal from dorsal orbital margin (char. 21.1); interpterygoid vacuity absent (char. 81.1); splenial entering mandibular symphysis (char. 88.0); and femur internal trochanter well developed (char. 203.0).
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Palatodonta was recovered as the sister-taxon of Eusaurosphargis.
source: Palatodonta was recovered as the sister-taxon of Eusaurosphargis.
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The clade comprising Palatodonta + Eusaurosphargis was recovered as the sister-group to Sauropterygia within Sauropterygomorpha.
source: The clade comprising Palatodonta + Eusaurosphargis was recovered as the sister-group to Sauropterygia within Sauropterygomorpha tax. nov. (see above).
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Helveticosaurus was recovered as the sister-group of Sauropterygomorpha.
source: Helveticosaurus was recovered as the sister-group of Sauropterygomorpha
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The clade comprising Helveticosaurus + Sauropterygomorpha is supported by six unambiguous synapomorphies.
source: the clade comprising Helveticosaurus + Sauropterygomorpha is supported by the following six unambiguous synapomorphies: preorbital and postorbital regions of skull of subequal length (ch. 1.0); transverse processes of neural arches of the dorsal region distinctly elongated (ch. 124.1); scapula with a constriction separating a ventral glenoidal portion from a posteriorly directed dorsal wing (ch. 154.2); distal tarsal I absent (ch. 184.1); total number of tarsal ossifications less than four (ch. 192.1); total number of carpal ossifications two (char. 194.2).
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Within Diapsida, the clade comprising Helveticosaurus + Sauropterygomorpha was recovered as forming a clade with Ichthyosauromorpha, Thalattosauria and Archosauromorpha.
source: Within Diapsida, the clade comprising Helveticosaurus + Sauropterygomorpha was recovered as forming a clade with Ichthyosauromorpha, Thalattosauria and Archosauromorpha, a result similar to that recovered in some other recent broad-scale analyses of diapsid phylogenetic interrelationships (Chen et al., 2014a; Neenan et al., 2015; Martínez et al., 2021; Simões et al., 2022).
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis and comparison with other studies.

claim: Sauropterygomorpha, Ichthyosauromorpha, Thalattosauria, Archosauromorpha, and Testudines were recovered within a monophyletic Archelosauria.
source: The three major marine reptile clades (Sauropterygomorpha, Ichthyosauromorpha and Thalattosauria), Archosauromorpha, and Testudines were recovered within a monophyletic Archelosauria
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Archelosauria is supported by four unambiguous synapomorphies: frontal with distinct posterolateral processes, frontal anterior margins oblique, forming an angle of at least 30 degrees with long axis of the skull, interclavicle anterior process or triangle conspicuously present, and upper temporal fossae present and distinctly smaller than the orbit.
source: supported by four unambiguous synapomorphies – frontal with distinct posterolateral processes (ch. 26.1), frontal anterior margins oblique, forming an angle of at least 30 degrees with long axis of the skull (ch. 27.1), interclavicle anterior process or triangle conspicuously present (ch. 157.0), and upper temporal fossae present and distinctly smaller than the orbit (ch. 207.3).
evidence: This is the result of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Prosaurosphargis extends the fossil record of Saurosphargidae back by approximately 3 Ma from the Middle (Pelsonian) to the Early (Olenekian) Triassic.
source: Prosaurosphargis represents the stratigraphically oldest occurrence of Saurosphargidae, extending their fossil record back by approximately 3 Ma from the Middle (Pelsonian) to the Early (Olenekian) Triassic (Figure 9).
evidence: This is based on stratigraphic data and comparison with other saurosphargid occurrences.

claim: Saurosphargids are the fourth major marine reptile lineage known from the Early Triassic Nanzhang-Yuan'an fauna.
source: Saurosphargids are thus the fourth major marine reptile lineage known from the Early Triassic Nanzhang-Yuan'an fauna, which also includes as many as seven species of hupehsuchians (Chen et al., 2016a; Qiao et al., 2019), one species of ichthyosauriforms (Chen et al., 2013), and three taxa representing the sauropterygian lineage leading to Eosauropterygia – Hanosaurus, Lariosaurus sanxiaensis, and Pomolispondylus (Young, 1965; Rieppel, 1998a; Li and Liu, 2020; Cheng et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on the fossil record and citations to previous studies.

claim: Prosaurosphargis is one of the larger marine reptiles known from the Nanzhang-Yuan'an fauna, measuring approximately 1.5 m in total body length.
source: Measuring approximately 1.5 m in total body length, Prosaurosphargis is one of the larger marine reptiles known from this ecosystem, smaller only than a large unidentified eosauropterygian (body length of 3–4 m; Chen et al., 2014b, Chen et al., 2016a) and an indeterminate hupehsuchian (body length of ~2.3 m; Qiao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on body size estimates and comparison with other fauna members.

claim: The presence of several marine reptiles representing a broad range of body sizes in the Nazhang-Yuan'an fauna supports the view of a rapid diversification of predators in the immediate aftermath of the PTME and high predation pressure in shallow marine ecosystems in the Early Triassic.
source: The presence in the Nazhang-Yuan'an fauna of several marine reptiles representing a broad range of body sizes (~0.25–4.00 m; Chen et al., 2014b; Qiao et al., 2019) and displaying various ecomorphological adaptations supports the view of a rapid diversification of predators in the immediate aftermath of the PTME and high predation pressure in shallow marine ecosystems in the Early Triassic (Chen et al., 2014b; Chen et al., 2014c; Li and Liu, 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the diversity and body size range of marine reptiles in the fauna.

claim: Eusaurosphargis and Palatodonta likely represent the morphology of the last common terrestrial ancestor of sauropterygians.
source: Our phylogenetic analysis suggests that Eusaurosphargis and Palatodonta likely represent the morphology of the last common terrestrial ancestor of sauropterygians
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis results.

claim: The status of Eusaurosphargis + Palatodonta as the sister-group to Sauropterygia is corroborated by the presence in Eusaurosphargis of morphological features otherwise known exclusively in sauropterygians: a clavicle applied to the medial surface of the scapula and a pectoral fenestration.
source: The status of Eusaurosphargis + Palatodonta as the sister-group to Sauropterygia is corroborated by the presence in Eusaurosphargis of morphological features otherwise known exclusively in sauropterygians: a clavicle applied to the medial surface of the scapula and a pectoral fenestration (Scheyer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Scheyer et al., 2017 and morphological comparison.

claim: Eusaurosphargis and Sauropterygia share a similar foot morphology with metatarsal I being proximodistally much shorter than metatarsal IV and metatarsal V being long and slender.
source: Furthermore, Eusaurosphargis and Sauropterygia also share a similar foot morphology with metatarsal I being proximodistally much shorter than metatarsal IV and metatarsal V being long and slender (see above).
evidence: This is based on morphological comparison.

claim: Helveticosaurus likely convergently evolved an aquatic lifestyle.
source: Consequently, we interpret Helveticosaurus as a representative of a lineage closely related to Sauropterygomorpha but lying outside of it, that likely convergently evolved an aquatic lifestyle.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis and morphological features.

claim: A terrestrial lifestyle was previously proposed for Eusaurosphargis on the basis of manus and pes anatomy and bone microanatomy.
source: A terrestrial lifetyle was previously proposed for Eusaurosphargis on the basis of manus and pes anatomy and bone microanatomy (Scheyer et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Scheyer et al., 2017.

claim: The femur of Eusaurosphargis is longer than its humerus (humerus:femur ratio ~0.89), which indicates hindlimb dominance characteristic of a terrestrial lifestyle.
source: and the femur of Eusaurosphargis is longer than its humerus (humerus:femur ratio ~0.89; Scheyer et al., 2017), which indicates hindlimb dominance characteristic of a terrestrial lifestyle (Motani and Vermeij, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Scheyer et al., 2017 and Motani and Vermeij, 2021.

claim: Palatodonta and Eusaurosphargis were terrestrial reptiles, likely representing the morphology of the last common terrestrial ancestor of Sauropterygia.
source: All this evidence strongly suggests that Palatodonta and Eusaurosphargis were terrestrial reptiles, likely representing the morphology of the last common terrestrial ancestor of Sauropterygia.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: It is very likely that Palatodonta is a junior synonym of Eusaurosphargis.
source: Because postcranial remains referable to Eusaurosphargis were also reported from the type locality of Palatodonta, including a Palatodonta-like dentary preserved in close association with typical Eusaurosphargis-like vertebrae (Scheyer et al., 2019; Willemse et al., 2019), it is very likely that Palatodonta is a junior synonym of Eusaurosphargis
evidence: This is inferred from the association of Palatodonta-like and Eusaurosphargis-like remains at the same locality.

claim: Atopodentatus and the early-diverging placodonts Placodus and Paraplacodus possess a humerus which is longer than the femur, indicating a high level of adaptation to an aquatic lifestyle.
source: Atopodentatus and the early-diverging placodonts Placodus and Paraplacodus possess a humerus which is longer than the femur, indicating a high level of adaptation to an aquatic lifestyle (Motani and Vermeij, 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Motani and Vermeij, 2021.

claim: Atopodentatus and placodonts possess a massive femoral fourth trochanter and an ilium with a well-developed iliac blade, indicating that the hindlimbs were likely still important in locomotion at the bottom of the sea floor and/or on shore in a marginal marine environment.
source: but they also possess a massive femoral fourth trochanter and an ilium with a well-developed iliac blade (Jiang et al., 2008; Cheng et al., 2014). These features indicate that the hindlimbs in both Atopodentatus and placodonts were likely still important in locomotion at the bottom of the sea floor and/or on shore in a marginal marine environment
evidence: This is inferred from morphological features and supported by citations.

claim: Placodontiforms have a slightly lower degree of adaptation to an aquatic lifestyle than saurosphargids and eosauropterygians.
source: and suggest a slightly lower degree of adaptation to an aquatic lifestyle in placodontiforms than in saurosphargids and eosauropterygians, in which the fourth trochanter is more reduced (Rieppel, 2000a; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from morphological comparison and supported by citations.

claim: The sister-group relationships of Atopodentatus and placodonts might explain the absence of placodont fossils in Early Triassic fossil horizons worldwide.
source: The sister-group relationships of Atopodentatus and placodonts might also explain the absence of placodont fossils in Early Triassic fossil horizons worldwide.
evidence: This is speculation based on the phylogenetic results.

claim: It is possible that the lineage leading to placodonts was represented in the Early Triassic by reptiles morphologically more similar to Atopodentatus than to placodonts and that the specialised placodont body plan did not evolve until the Middle Triassic.
source: It is possible that the lineage leading to placodonts was represented in the Early Triassic by reptiles morphologically more similar to Atopodentatus than to placodonts and that the specialised placodont body plan did not evolve until the Middle Triassic.
evidence: This is speculation based on the phylogenetic results.

claim: Pomolispondylus possesses dorsal transverse processes that are relatively short mediolaterally and broad anteroposteriorly, more similar to Lariosaurus sanxiaensis and Hanosaurus than to saurosphargids.
source: Such a phylogenetic position is supported by the presence in Pomolispondylus of dorsal transverse processes that are relatively short mediolaterally and broad anteroposteriorly, more similar in proportions to the dorsal transverse processes of Lariosaurus sanxiaensis (Li and Liu, 2020) and Hanosaurus (Wang et al., 2022) – two other representatives of the grade leading to Eosauropterygia – than to the mediolaterally broad and anteroposteriorly narrow dorsal neural spines of saurosphargids (Figure 3; Li et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on morphological comparison and supported by citations.

claim: Pomolispondylus possesses rows of rudimentary osteoderms on its body flanks, which are much more reduced than those present in Eusaurosphargis, early-diverging placodonts and saurosphargids.
source: Furthermore, Pomolispondylus possesses rows of rudimentary osteoderms on its body flanks, which are much more reduced than those present in Eusaurosphargis, early-diverging placodonts and saurosphargids (Klein and Scheyer, 2013; Li et al., 2014; Scheyer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on morphological comparison and supported by citations.

claim: The osteoderms in Pomolispondylus likely represent a late stage of osteoderm reduction in the lineage leading to Eosauropterygia.
source: Therefore, the osteoderms in Pomolispondylus likely represent a late stage of osteoderm reduction in the lineage leading to Eosauropterygia, rather than the first stages of osteoderm development in the saurosphargid lineage.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic position and morphology of Pomolispondylus.

claim: The anteriorly and posteriorly weakly emarginated coracoid of the type specimen of Hanosaurus more closely resembles that of Corosaurus than the sub-oval coracoid present in the referred specimen of Hanosaurus.
source: Taxonomic distinction of both specimens is supported by the fact that the anteriorly and posteriorly weakly emarginated coracoid of the type specimen of Hanosaurus (Figure 7G and H; Rieppel, 1998a; pers. obs. of IVPP V 3231) more closely resembles that of Corosaurus than the sub-oval coracoid present in the referred specimen of Hanosaurus (Figure 7I; Wang et al., 2022)
evidence: This is based on morphological comparison of specimens.

claim: The referred specimen of Hanosaurus likely does not represent Hanosaurus, but is probably closely related or even referable to Lariosaurus sanxiaensis.
source: which likely does not represent Hanosaurus, but is probably closely related or even referable to Lariosaurus sanxiaensis (Figure 7J; Chen et al., 2016b; Li and Liu, 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from morphological comparison.

claim: The results of the phylogenetic analysis differ significantly from the results of Wang et al., 2022.
source: The results of our phylogenetic analysis differ significantly from the results of a phylogenetic analysis recently published by Wang et al., 2022, in which Hanosaurus was recovered as the sister-group to a clade comprising Saurosphargidae + Sauropterygia within a monophyletic Sauropterygiformes.
evidence: This is a comparison of phylogenetic results.

claim: Wang et al., 2022 used 16 outgroup taxa (15 marine reptiles and a single terrestrial reptile), representing five major reptile lineages.
source: Wang et al., 2022 used 16 outgroup (non-sauropterygiform) taxa (15 marine reptiles and a single terrestrial reptile), representing five major reptile lineages
evidence: This is factual information about the Wang et al., 2022 study.

claim: The current study included 40 outgroup taxa (19 terrestrial and 21 aquatic reptiles), representing 23 major reptile lineages.
source: whereas our study included 40 outgroup (non-sauropterygomorph) taxa (19 terrestrial and 21 aquatic reptiles), representing 23 major reptile lineages.
evidence: This is factual information about the current study.

claim: The inclusion of only a single terrestrial outgroup taxon in Wang et al., 2022 is problematic because Youngina likely represents a taxon rather distantly related to the Mesozoic marine reptile clade which includes Sauropterygia.
source: The inclusion of only a single terrestrial outgroup taxon – Youngina – in the analysis of Wang et al., 2022 is problematic because Youngina likely represents a taxon rather distantly related to the Mesozoic marine reptile clade which includes Sauropterygia (Figure 8; see also Simões et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic relationships.

claim: A phylogenetic analysis containing a single, distantly related outgroup taxon will likely fail to adequately capture important character transformation sequences.
source: Distantly related taxa likely share fewer character states with derived taxa (homoplasy accumulation through time), so a phylogenetic analysis containing a single, distantly related outgroup taxon will likely fail to adequately capture important character transformation sequences, in contrast to a phylogenetic analysis in which outgroups are more comprehensively sampled (Wilberg, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilberg, 2015.

claim: Greater character sampling has been demonstrated as an important factor increasing the accuracy of phylogenetic reconstructions.
source: Greater character sampling has been demonstrated as an important factor increasing the accuracy of phylogenetic reconstructions (Wiens, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wiens, 2006.

claim: The different topologies recovered by the current study and Wang et al., 2022 are likely partially a consequence of differences in character scoring.
source: The different topologies recovered by both studies are likely also partially a consequence of differences in character scoring.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the two studies.

claim: The early evolution of sauropterygians first involved diversification within a shallow marine environment and exploration of various food resources.
source: The topology recovered by our phylogenetic analysis demonstrates that the early evolution of sauropterygians first involved diversification within a shallow marine environment and exploration of various food resources, as evidenced by the disparate ecologies exhibited by Atopodentatus (herbivore), placodonts (durophages), saurosphargids, and early-diverging members of the eosauropterygian lineage (likely feeding on fish and invertebrates).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis and ecological interpretations.

claim: Three key episodes can be identified in the evolution of the eosauropterygian body plan.
source: Three key episodes can be identified in the evolution of the eosauropterygian body plan (Figure 10).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The first episode in the evolution of the eosauropterygian body plan, represented by Pomolispondylus, involved a reduction of osteoderms and shortening of the transverse processes of the dorsal neural spines.
source: The first, represented by Pomolispondylus, involved a reduction of osteoderms and shortening of the transverse processes of the dorsal neural spines, features well-developed in Eusaurosphargis, placodonts and saurosphargids.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis and morphological comparison.

claim: The second episode in the evolution of the eosauropterygian body plan, exemplified by Majiashanosaurus and the referred specimen of Hanosaurus, involved complete reduction of osteoderms.
source: Majiashanosaurus and the referred specimen of Hanosaurus exemplify the second episode, in which osteoderms underwent complete reduction.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis and morphological comparison.

claim: The type specimen of Hanosaurus represents the earliest stage of the evolution of the characteristic eosauropterygian pectoral girdle morphology with an anteriorly and posteriorly emarginated coracoid.
source: The type specimen of Hanosaurus represents the earliest stage of the evolution of the characteristic eosauropterygian pectoral girdle morphology with an anteriorly and posteriorly emarginated coracoid that ultimately allowed eosauropterygians to become efficient, paraxial swimmers.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis and morphological comparison.

claim: The presence of the stratigraphically oldest saurosphargid and representatives of the lineage leading to Eosauropterygia in the Early–Middle Triassic of South China indicates that sauropterygians likely originated and underwent rapid diversification in South China in the aftermath of the end-Smithian extinction.
source: The presence of the stratigraphically oldest saurosphargid (Prosaurosphargis), stratigraphically oldest representatives of the lineage leading to Eosauropterygia (Pomolispondylus, Hanosaurus, Majiashanosaurus), and the earliest-diverging placodontiform Atopodentatus in the Early–Middle Triassic of South China (Figure 9) indicates that sauropterygians likely originated and underwent rapid diversification in South China in the aftermath of the end-Smithian extinction, similar to ichthyosauromorphs (Motani et al., 2017; Moon and Stubbs, 2020)
evidence: This is inferred from stratigraphic and phylogenetic data and supported by citations.

claim: Dermal armour was likely an important preadaptation that allowed colonisation of the shallow marine realm by a Eusaurosphargis-like ancestor.
source: Dermal armour was likely an important preadaptation that allowed colonisation of the shallow marine realm by a Eusaurosphargis-like ancestor, enabling it to counteract buoyancy and walk on the bottom of the shallow sea in search of food (Houssaye, 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis and functional morphology, supported by citation.

claim: Elaboration of the dermal armour occurred in the shallow marine placodonts and saurosphargids, perhaps as a response to predation pressure.
source: Elaboration of the dermal armour occurred in the shallow marine placodonts and saurosphargids, perhaps as a response to predation pressure (Liu et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014b; Qiao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis and supported by citations.

claim: The reduction and complete loss of dermal armour occurred in the lineage leading to Eosauropterygia, and was likely associated with the evolution of active predation, an efficient swimming style and increasing adaptation to a pelagic lifestyle.
source: The reduction and complete loss of dermal armour then occurred in the lineage leading to Eosauropterygia, and was likely associated with the evolution of active predation, an efficient swimming style and increasing adaptation to a pelagic lifestyle.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis and functional morphology.

claim: The evolution of the sauropterygian body plan demonstrates striking parallels with the evolution of the body plan of ichthyosaurs.
source: The evolution of the sauropterygian body plan demonstrates striking parallels with the evolution of the body plan of another important group of Mesozoic marine reptiles – the ichthyosaurs.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of evolutionary patterns.

claim: Early-diverging representatives of Ichthyosauromorpha – hupehsuchians and omphalosaurids – possessed a covering of osteoderms superficially similar to that present in Eusaurosphargis, early-diverging placodonts, and saurosphargids.
source: Early-diverging representatives of Ichthyosauromorpha – hupehsuchians and omphalosaurids – also possesed a covering of osteoderms superficially similar to that present in Eusaurosphargis, early-diverging placodonts, and saurosphargids (Chen et al., 2014b; Jiang et al., 2016; Qiao et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2014b; Jiang et al., 2016; Qiao et al., 2022.

claim: In the ichthyosauromorph lineage, the osteoderm covering was completely lost in Chaohusaurus, a basal ichthyosauriform that evolved an anguilliform mode of swimming and most likely a pelagic lifestyle.
source: In the ichthyosauromorph lineage, the osteoderm covering was completely lost in Chaohusaurus, a basal ichthyosauriform that evolved an anguilliform mode of swimming and most likely a pelagic lifestyle (Motani et al., 1996; Nakajima et al., 2014; Qiao et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Motani et al., 1996; Nakajima et al., 2014; Qiao et al., 2022.

claim: The evolutionary reduction of dermal armour in both sauropterygians and ichthyosauromorphs followed a similar pattern, probably in response to increasing adaptation to an aquatic lifestyle.
source: This indicates that the evolutionary reduction of dermal armour in both sauropterygians and ichthyosauromorphs followed a similar pattern, probably in response to increasing adaptation to an aquatic lifestyle.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of evolutionary patterns.

claim: The dermal body armour could have been a possible prerequisite (preadaptation) for the invasion of the shallow marine realm in different diapsid clades.
source: These evolutionary parallels seem to demonstrate that the dermal body armour could have been a possible prerequsite (preadaptation) for the invasion of the shallow marine realm in different diapsid clades, which allowed for buoyancy reduction and exploration of the shallow marine environment in search of food.
evidence: This is speculation based on the evolutionary parallels observed.

claim: The current phylogenetic analysis is one of only two phylogenetic analyses based on a morphology-only dataset of Diapsida that recovers a close relationship between Archosauromorpha and Testudines within a monophyletic Archelosauria.
source: Our phylogenetic analysis is thus far one of only two phylogenetic analyses based on a morphology-only dataset of Diapsida that recovers a close relationship between Archosauromorpha and Testudines within a monophyletic Archelosauria (Figure 8) (see also Simões et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a comparison with other phylogenetic studies.

claim: The current analysis recovers Eunotosaurus outside of Sauria, in agreement with Simões et al., 2022, but in contrast to other recent phylogenetic analyses.
source: Furthermore, our analysis recovers Eunotosaurus from the Permian of South Africa outside of Sauria (Figure 8), which is in agreement with the results obtained by Simões et al., 2022, but in contrast to all other recent phylogenetic analyses focussing on the phylogenetic interrelationships among Reptilia, which recovered Eunotosaurus as a stem turtle (Lyson et al., 2013; Bever et al., 2015; Li et al., 2018; Schoch and Sues, 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison with other phylogenetic studies.

claim: The characteristic morphological features of the skull and postcranial skeleton shared between Eunotosaurus and early turtles evolved convergently in both taxa.
source: This indicates that the characteristic morphological features of the skull and postcranial skeleton shared between Eunotosaurus and early turtles, such as elongate vertebrae and broadened ribs, evolved convergently in both taxa.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic results.

claim: Innovations of the cranium linked with the evolution of sensory organs and the feeding apparatus, as well as changes in locomotion, perhaps underlie the evolutionary success of archelosaurian reptiles.
source: This demonstrates that innovations of the cranium linked with the evolution of sensory organs and the feeding apparatus, as well as changes in locomotion, perhaps underlie the evolutionary success of archelosaurian reptiles.
evidence: This is speculation based on the synapomorphies supporting Archelosauria.

claim: The study emphasises the importance of broad taxonomic sampling in reconstructing phylogenetic relationships among extinct taxa.
source: Our study provides evidence for the rapid diversification of sauropterygians in the aftermath of the Permo-Triassic mass extinction event and emphasises the importance of broad taxonomic sampling in reconstructing phylogenetic relationships among extinct taxa.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's methodology and results.

claim: Specimen HFUT YZSB-19-109 was scored into a modified version of a data matrix published by Qiao et al., 2022.
source: In order to investigate the phylogenetic position of Prosaurosphargis yingzishanensis, specimen HFUT YZSB-19-109 was scored into a modified version of a data matrix focusing on the phylogenetic interrelationships between the major groups of diapsid reptiles published by Qiao et al., 2022
evidence: This is a description of the methods used.

claim: The data matrix contains 57 OTUs scored for a total of 221 characters.
source: The data matrix contains 57 OTUs (Operational Taxonomic Units) scored for a total of 221 characters
evidence: This is a description of the data matrix used.

claim: 10 OTUs were added to the original dataset of Qiao et al., 2022.
source: In addition to Prosaurosphargis, 10 OTUs were added to the original dataset of Qiao et al., 2022
evidence: This is a description of modifications to the data matrix.

claim: Parsimony analysis was performed in TNT 1.5 using a Traditional Search algorithm.
source: Parsimony analysis of the data matrix was performed in TNT 1.5 (Goloboff and Catalano, 2016) using a Traditional Search algorithm (random seed = 1, replications of Wagner trees = 1000, number of trees saved per replication = 10), followed by an additional round of TBR branch-swapping.
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis methods.

claim: All characters were treated as equally weighted and unordered.
source: All characters were treated as equally weighted and unordered.
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis methods.
